title: Herb-Roasted Turkey Thighs with Pan Gravy
description: Thanksgiving for a small table without a whole bird: turkey thighs roast over onions, carrots and celery, and the drippings become a proper gravy. Serves 6 for about $2.50 a person.
equipment: fat separator or glass measuring cup
notes: Four thighs give about 2 pounds of meat, enough for 6 plates alongside stuffing and sides, and dark meat stays moist even when dinner runs late. A 3-pound bone-in turkey breast works the same way: roast it on the vegetables for about 1 1/2 hours, until the thickest part reads 165°F. Thaw frozen turkey in the refrigerator for 1 to 2 days, never on the counter. For dairy-free, use olive oil in the herb rub and turkey fat alone for the roux; for gluten-free gravy, skip the flour and simmer the juices with 2 tbsp cornstarch stirred into 1/4 cup cold broth, which removes wheat. Save the bones in the freezer for broth. Refrigerate meat and gravy within 2 hours; they keep 4 days, or freeze sliced meat covered in gravy for up to 3 months. Reheat covered with a splash of broth to 165°F and bring leftover gravy to a full boil.

ingredients.name: bone-in, skin-on turkey thighs (about 3 1/2 lb total)
yellow onion, cut into thick wedges

instructions: Pat the turkey thighs very dry with paper towels and season all over with 2 tsp of the salt and the pepper. If you have time, refrigerate them uncovered on a rack for 4 to 24 hours; the drier skin browns and crisps far better.

Heat the oven to 375°F. Mash the butter with the thyme, rosemary and garlic. Slide your fingers under the skin of each thigh to loosen it, push half the herb butter underneath, and rub the rest over the top.
Scatter the onion, carrot and celery in the roasting pan and pour in 1/2 cup of the broth. Set the thighs skin side up on the vegetables so they roast above the liquid.

Roast for 75 to 90 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part, not touching bone, reads at least 165°F. Thighs are most tender at 175 to 180°F. If the skin browns before the meat is done, tent it loosely with foil.

Move the thighs to a cutting board and let them rest for 15 minutes. Lift the vegetables onto a platter. Pour the pan juices into a fat separator, then set the roasting pan over medium heat, add 1/2 cup water, and scrape up the browned bits; add this to the juices and let everything settle for 5 minutes.

Spoon 3 tbsp of the clear fat into a medium saucepan over medium heat, topping up with butter if you are short. Whisk in the flour and cook for 2 minutes, until it smells toasty and turns light brown.

Slowly whisk in the defatted pan juices and the remaining 2 cups broth. Simmer for 5 to 8 minutes, whisking often, until the gravy coats a spoon. Stir in the vinegar and season with the remaining salt to taste.
Pull the skin off in pieces and slice the meat from the bones. Serve the turkey with the roasted vegetables and hot gravy.

title: Maple-Mustard Roast Pork Shoulder with Potatoes and Carrots
description: A boneless pork shoulder roasts low and covered until tender, then takes a glossy maple-mustard glaze while potatoes and carrots cook in its juices. Three pounds feeds 8 for about $2 a plate.
notes: Pork is safe at 145°F, but shoulder needs to pass 190°F for its connective tissue to soften enough to slice tender; if a fork meets resistance, give it 15 more minutes covered. A bone-in shoulder works too: add about 30 minutes to the covered roasting time. Watch the glaze in the last minutes, because maple syrup goes from dark amber to burnt quickly; tent the roast with foil if the edges darken too fast. Whole-grain mustard is usually gluten-free, but check the label if you cook for someone with celiac disease. Water can stand in for the cider with a little less sweetness. Leftover pork makes good sandwiches, fried rice or a breakfast hash. Refrigerate within 2 hours; it keeps 4 days, or freeze slices with some pan juices for up to 3 months. Reheat covered with a splash of water to 165°F.

ingredients.name: boneless pork shoulder, tied or netted
russet or yukon gold potatoes, cut into 2-inch chunks
carrot, peeled and cut into 2-inch lengths
chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, for serving

instructions: Stir together 2 tsp of the salt, the pepper, thyme, smoked paprika, allspice and garlic, and rub the mixture all over the pork. Let it sit at room temperature for 30 minutes while the oven heats, or refrigerate it overnight for deeper seasoning.
Heat the oven to 325°F. Set the pork fat side up in the roasting pan, pour the cider around it, and cover the pan tightly with foil. Roast for 2 hours.

Toss the potatoes, carrots and onion with the olive oil and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Uncover the pork, scatter the vegetables around it in the pan juices, and roast uncovered for 1 hour, turning the vegetables once halfway.

Whisk the maple syrup, mustard and vinegar in a small bowl. Raise the oven to 425°F. Brush half the glaze over the pork and roast for 15 minutes, then brush on the rest and roast 10 to 15 minutes more, until the glaze is lacquered and dark in spots, the vegetables are browned and tender, and the pork reads 190 to 195°F with a fork sliding in easily.

Tent the pork with foil and rest it for 15 minutes. Remove the string, slice across the grain about 1/2 inch thick, and serve with the vegetables, spooning the pan juices over everything. Scatter parsley on top if you like.

title: Butternut Squash and White Bean Stew with Kale and Rosemary
description: A thick Tuscan-inspired stew of tender squash, cannellini beans and kale, built on garlic, rosemary and a little tomato. Six big bowls for about $2 each, and it tastes even better the next day.
equipment: large Dutch oven or heavy pot
notes: To peel the squash more easily, microwave it whole for 2 minutes, cut off both ends, then use a Y-shaped peeler. Sweet potatoes can replace the squash, and baby spinach can replace the kale if you stir it in during the last 2 minutes. Mashing some of the beans is what makes the stew thick without cream; if it gets too thick on standing, loosen it with water or broth. Grated parmesan on top or crusty bread on the side are good, but they add milk and wheat. Refrigerate within 2 hours; the stew keeps 5 days and freezes for 3 months, though the kale softens. Reheat to 165°F, stirring, and add a squeeze of lemon to wake it up.

ingredients.name: extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for serving
butternut squash (about 2 1/2 lb), peeled, seeded and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
cannellini beans (15 oz), drained and rinsed
lacinato or curly kale, stems removed, leaves chopped

instructions: Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, celery and 1/2 tsp of the salt and cook, stirring now and then, for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and the onion is translucent.
Add the garlic, rosemary and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes more, until it darkens to brick red and starts to stick.

Add the squash, crushed tomatoes, broth, bay leaf and the remaining 1 tsp salt. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 15 to 20 minutes, until a knife slides into the squash easily but the cubes still hold their shape.
Mash about 1 cup of the beans with a fork in a small bowl. Stir the mashed and whole beans into the pot and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the stew thickens.
Stir in the kale and simmer for 5 to 7 minutes, until it is tender and dark green. Remove the bay leaf, stir in the lemon juice, and season with pepper and more salt to taste.
Ladle into bowls and finish each with a thin drizzle of olive oil.

title: Day-Old Bread Stuffing with Celery, Onion and Fresh Herbs
description: A classic baked stuffing made from a stale loaf, butter, onion, celery and herbs, crisp on top and soft inside. A Thanksgiving side for 8 for about $10, and a good home for bread that would otherwise go to waste.
notes: Bake stuffing in a dish rather than inside the bird: inside, it cannot reach 165°F before the meat overcooks. Any plain bread works, including sandwich bread, rolls and saved heels, but skip sweet breads. Vegetable broth makes it vegetarian; olive oil in place of butter makes it dairy-free; leaving out the eggs gives a looser, crumblier stuffing and removes the egg allergen; gluten-free bread removes wheat. To get ahead, toss the bread with the cooked vegetables up to a day early and refrigerate, then add the egg and broth just before baking and allow 10 extra minutes. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; they keep 4 days or freeze for 2 months. Reheat covered at 350°F, with a splash of broth, to 165°F.

ingredients.name: stale crusty country bread, cut into 3/4-inch cubes (about 12 cups)
unsalted butter (85 g), plus more for the dish

instructions: Heat the oven to 375°F. If the bread is not fully dry, spread the cubes on a rimmed baking sheet and bake for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once, until dry and crisp at the edges. Tip them into a large bowl.

Melt the butter in a 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Add the onion, celery, carrot and salt and cook, stirring now and then, for 10 to 12 minutes, until soft and lightly golden. Add the garlic, thyme and rosemary and cook 1 minute more.

Scrape the vegetables and butter over the bread, add the parsley and pepper, and toss well. Whisk the eggs with 2 cups of the broth, pour it over the bread, and fold gently until evenly moistened. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then add the remaining broth if dry patches remain; it should be moist but not soupy.
Butter the baking dish and spread the stuffing in it loosely, without packing it down. Cover with foil and bake for 25 minutes.
Uncover and bake for 20 to 25 minutes more, until the top is deep golden and crisp and the center reads 165°F on an instant-read thermometer. Let it rest for 5 minutes before serving.

title: Garlic Mashed Potatoes for a Crowd
description: Potatoes simmered with whole garlic cloves and mashed with warm milk, butter and a little sour cream: creamy, not gluey. Five pounds serves 10 for about $6, and they hold well in a busy holiday kitchen.
notes: Yukon Golds give a dense, creamy mash and russets a lighter, fluffier one; a mix of the two is good. Never use a blender or food processor, which turns potatoes gluey. To hold them, cover the pot and set it over a pan of barely simmering water for up to 1 hour, or keep them in a slow cooker on WARM for up to 2 hours, stirring in a splash of warm milk before serving. You can make them 2 days ahead: refrigerate, then reheat covered in a 350°F oven with a little milk for about 30 minutes, to 165°F. For dairy-free, use olive oil and unsweetened nut-free plant milk and skip the sour cream, which removes milk. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; they keep 4 days and make good potato cakes or a pie topping. They freeze for 1 month, a little grainier after thawing.

ingredients.name: russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 2-inch chunks
kosher salt, for the cooking water
unsalted butter (113 g), cut into pieces
kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions: Put the potatoes and garlic in an 8-quart pot, cover with cold water by 1 inch, and add the 2 tbsp salt. Starting in cold water lets the chunks cook evenly to the center.
Bring to a boil over high heat, then lower to a steady simmer and cook for 18 to 22 minutes, until a paring knife slides through the largest piece with no resistance.
While the potatoes cook, warm the milk and butter in a small saucepan over low heat until the butter melts; do not let it boil.
Drain the potatoes and garlic well in a colander. Return them to the hot pot over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes, shaking the pot, to steam off the last of the water.

Mash the potatoes and garlic, or press them through a ricer, until smooth. Stir in the warm milk mixture in 2 additions, then the sour cream, 1 tsp salt and plenty of pepper. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Spoon into a warm bowl and top with the scallions and a pat of butter if you like.

title: Honey-Thyme Roasted Carrots with Lemon
description: Carrots roast hot until their edges caramelize, then take a quick honey-thyme glaze and a squeeze of lemon. Two pounds serves 6 for about $3, a bright side next to rich holiday dishes.
notes: Cut thick carrots in half lengthwise so all the pieces are about the same size and finish together. If the oven is already set to 375°F for a turkey or stuffing, roast them there and add 10 to 15 minutes. Honey can scorch, which is why it goes on only for the last minutes; pull the pan if the glaze starts to smoke. Pure maple syrup in place of the honey makes the dish vegan. Leftovers are good cold in grain salads or blended into soup. Refrigerate within 2 hours; they keep 4 days. Reheat on a sheet pan at 400°F for 5 to 8 minutes; freezing makes them soft, so skip it.

ingredients.name: carrot, peeled, halved lengthwise if thick, cut into 3-inch lengths
chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, for serving

instructions: Heat the oven to 425°F with a rack in the center and line a rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper.
Toss the carrots with the olive oil, salt and pepper right on the baking sheet. Spread them in a single layer, cut sides down, with a little space between pieces so they brown instead of steam.
Roast for 20 minutes, until the undersides are browned in spots.

Stir the honey, thyme and red pepper flakes together in a small bowl, warming the honey for 10 seconds in the microwave if it is thick. Drizzle it over the carrots, toss, and roast 8 to 10 minutes more, until glazed, tender when pierced with a knife, and caramelized at the edges.
Toss the hot carrots with the lemon zest and juice, pile them onto a platter, and scatter the parsley over the top.

title: Green Beans with Crispy Shallots and Garlic
description: Fresh green beans blanched bright, tossed in shallot-scented oil with garlic and lemon, then topped with shallots fried until crisp. All the crunch of the casserole without the canned soup, for 8 people at about $6.
notes: Starting the shallots in cold oil lets them brown slowly and evenly; they keep darkening after they leave the pan, so pull them at light golden brown. Keep children away from the hot oil and let it cool fully before moving the pan. The shallots stay crisp for 2 days in an airtight container at room temperature, and blanched beans keep 2 days refrigerated in a towel-lined container, so most of the work can happen ahead. Strain the leftover shallot oil and refrigerate it for up to 1 week; it makes a good vinaigrette. Frozen whole green beans work: skip the blanching and cook them from frozen in the skillet for 6 to 8 minutes. A tablespoon of butter adds milk, and toasted almonds add tree nuts. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; they keep 3 days, though the shallots soften.

ingredients.name: shallot (about 6 oz), thinly sliced into rings
kosher salt, for the cooking water
kosher salt, plus a pinch for the shallots

instructions: Put the shallots and oil in a cold small saucepan and set it over medium heat. Cook, stirring often, for 12 to 18 minutes as they bubble, until evenly light golden brown. Lift them out with a slotted spoon onto paper towels, sprinkle with a pinch of salt, and save the oil.

Bring a large pot of water to a boil with the 2 tbsp salt and set a large bowl of ice water nearby. Boil the green beans for 3 to 5 minutes, until bright green and crisp-tender. Drain, plunge them into the ice water for 2 minutes, then drain again and pat dry.

Heat 2 tbsp of the shallot oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and cook for about 30 seconds, until pale golden. Add the green beans, the 1/2 tsp salt and the red pepper flakes, and toss for 3 to 4 minutes, until hot through and lightly blistered.

Take the pan off the heat, toss the beans with the lemon juice and a few grinds of pepper, and taste for salt. Pile them onto a platter and top with the crispy shallots and a little flaky salt right before serving.

title: Sweet Potato, Apple and Sausage Hash with Fried Eggs
description: Diced sweet potato, tart apple and half a pound of Italian sausage brown together in one skillet, then eggs cook right on top. A fall breakfast for 4 at about $2 a plate.
equipment: 12-inch nonstick or cast-iron skillet with a lid
notes: Cook the sausage to 160°F, until no pink remains. Many sausages are gluten-free, but some contain breadcrumbs or other wheat fillers, so check the label if that matters at your table. Four slices of thick-cut bacon can replace the sausage, or leave it out and add a pinch more smoked paprika for a vegetarian hash. Firm-tart apples such as Granny Smith or Braeburn keep their shape best. For young children, older adults and anyone pregnant, cook the yolks until firm. The hash without eggs keeps 4 days in the refrigerator or 2 months in the freezer; refrigerate within 2 hours, reheat it in a skillet to 165°F, and fry fresh eggs on top.

ingredients.name: fresh sweet or hot italian pork sausage, casings removed
sweet potato (about 1 1/2 lb), peeled and cut into 1/2-inch dice
kosher salt, plus a pinch for the eggs
firm-tart apple, cored and cut into 1/2-inch dice
louisiana-style cayenne pepper hot sauce, for serving

instructions: Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add the sausage and break it into small pieces with a spatula. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until browned with no pink remaining and 160°F on an instant-read thermometer. Lift it onto a plate with a slotted spoon, leaving the fat behind.

Add the remaining oil, the sweet potato, onion and 3/4 tsp salt to the skillet and stir to coat. Spread in an even layer, add the water, cover, and cook over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until the sweet potato is nearly tender.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring only every 2 to 3 minutes so the cubes can brown, until crusty in places and fully tender.
Add the apple, smoked paprika, thyme and pepper and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until the apple is warm and just soft at the edges. Return the sausage to the pan, sprinkle with the vinegar, and toss.

Make 4 wells in the hash and crack an egg into each. Season the eggs with a pinch of salt, cover, and cook over medium-low heat for 4 to 6 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are done the way you like; allow 6 to 8 minutes for fully set yolks.
Serve straight from the skillet with scallions and hot sauce on the side.

title: Sweet Potato Pie with a Graham Cracker Crust
description: A smooth, warmly spiced Southern-style sweet potato pie in a press-in graham cracker crust, so there is no dough to roll. One pie serves 8 for about $5.
notes: Roasting the sweet potatoes instead of boiling them keeps the filling dense and sweet, not watery. Small cracks on top mean the pie baked a little long; pull it when the center still wobbles slightly, since it sets as it cools. Gluten-free graham crackers remove wheat. Full-fat coconut milk can replace the evaporated milk and coconut oil can replace the butter for a dairy-free pie, which removes milk. This is an egg-and-milk custard pie, so refrigerate it within 2 hours of cooling; covered, it keeps 4 days. The whole pie freezes, well wrapped, for 1 month; thaw it overnight in the refrigerator, knowing the crust softens a little.
instructions: Heat the oven to 400°F. Prick the sweet potatoes a few times with a fork and roast them on a foil-lined baking sheet for 45 to 60 minutes, until very soft and leaking syrup. Let them cool until you can handle them, then peel and measure 1 1/2 cups (about 340 g) of flesh. Lower the oven to 350°F.

Stir the graham cracker crumbs, granulated sugar, a pinch of the salt and the melted butter together until the mixture looks like wet sand. Press it firmly over the bottom and up the sides of a 9-inch pie plate, using the bottom of a measuring cup. Bake for 8 to 10 minutes, until fragrant and a shade darker, then cool for 10 minutes.

Blend the warm sweet potato with the softened butter in a food processor, or beat with a hand mixer, until completely smooth with no strings. Add the brown sugar, eggs, evaporated milk, vanilla, cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice and the rest of the salt and blend until smooth.

Pour the filling into the crust and set the pie on a baking sheet. Bake at 350°F for 45 to 55 minutes, until the edges are set and the center jiggles slightly, like gelatin, when you nudge the pan; an instant-read thermometer in the center should read about 175°F.
Cool the pie on a rack for at least 2 hours so it sets fully before slicing, then refrigerate. Serve it cool or at room temperature.

title: Cinnamon Apple Hand Pies with All-Butter Crust
description: Flaky all-butter pastry folded around cinnamon apples and baked until deep golden. Eight hand pies for about $5, easy to carry to a potluck and good at room temperature.
equipment: 5 1/2-inch saucer or bowl as a cutting guide
notes: Keep the butter and water very cold and stop mixing while you can still see pea-size pieces of butter; those pieces are what make the crust flaky. Without a food processor, cut the butter in with a pastry cutter or grate it frozen on a box grater. Granny Smith, Braeburn and Honeycrisp apples hold their shape; a mix tastes best. Brushing with milk instead of egg removes the egg allergen. The filling must be completely cool before it goes into the pastry, or it melts the butter. Freeze unbaked hand pies on the sheet, then bag them for up to 3 months and bake from frozen, adding 5 to 8 minutes. Baked hand pies keep 1 day covered at room temperature or 4 days in the refrigerator; warm them at 350°F for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp the crust.

ingredients.name: all-purpose flour (315 g), plus more for rolling
cold unsalted butter (226 g), cut into 1/2-inch cubes
ice water, plus 1 to 2 tbsp as needed
apple (about 1 1/4 lb), peeled, cored and cut into 1/4-inch dice
large egg, beaten with 1 tbsp water

instructions: Pulse the flour, 1 tbsp sugar and salt in a food processor. Add the cold butter and pulse until the pieces are about the size of peas. Drizzle in the ice water while pulsing in short bursts, just until the dough holds together when pinched. Divide it in half, flatten into 2 disks, wrap, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour or up to 2 days.

Melt the 1 tbsp butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the apples, brown sugar, cinnamon and lemon juice and cook, stirring, for 5 to 6 minutes, until the apples just soften and release their juice. Stir the cornstarch into 1 tbsp water, add it to the pan, and cook for 1 minute, until the juices turn thick and glossy. Spread the filling on a plate and let it cool completely.

On a lightly floured counter, roll one disk about 1/8 inch thick. Using a 5 1/2-inch saucer as a guide, cut out rounds, then press the scraps together, chill them briefly, and reroll once. Repeat with the second disk to make 8 rounds in all.

Spoon about 2 heaping tablespoons of filling onto one half of each round, leaving a 1/2-inch border. Brush the edge with egg wash, fold the dough over into a half-moon, and press the edges firmly with a fork to seal. Set the pies on a parchment-lined baking sheet and refrigerate for 20 minutes while the oven heats to 400°F.
Brush the tops with egg wash, sprinkle with the 2 tbsp sugar, and cut 2 small vents in each. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until deep golden brown and the filling bubbles at the vents.
Cool on the baking sheet for at least 15 minutes before eating; the filling stays very hot inside for a while.
